q: Analytical learning differs from inductive learning because it also takes as input:
explain: The domain theory lets it explain examples and justify generalisations.

q: A domain theory is perfect if it is:
explain: It must contain only true statements and cover every positive example of the target.
Analytical generalisation, by contrast, is justified deductively.

q: With a good domain theory, analytical learning can:
options: Generalise correctly from very few examples
Ignore all examples and still improve speed
explain: The explanation shows which features matter, so fewer examples are needed.

q: When the theory already implies the target, the learning problem becomes:
options: Rewriting the theory into an efficient, operational form
Finding new facts about the domain that were not implied
explain: Rewriting is what speeds up problem solving.

q: The main weakness of analytical learning is:
options: It can be misled by an incorrect theory
It can only use numeric attributes
explain: The generalisation is only as sound as the theory it is based on.

q: In chess, the rules of the game are an example of:
options: A perfect but computationally impractical domain theory
explain: The rules define the best move in principle, but calculating it is far too slow.

q: An analytical hypothesis must be consistent with:
options: Both the training data and the domain theory
explain: This is the defining requirement of the analytical learning problem.
